---
title: "Virtual Context and Durable Semantic Memory"
unit_id: "unit-14"

## The Patch That Remembered Too Much

The publication artifact from the previous chapter has been repaired. Its
private filesystem path is gone, and the conclusion once again says that the
bounded controller trial stopped after oscillation rather than claiming that
the controller safely detected it. The corrected page passes its target
checks.

The next morning, another worker is asked to prepare a short release note. It
retrieves a cached summary from the earlier attempt. That summary still
contains the private path and the word “safely.” A policy record revoking use
of the raw trace exists in the repository, but the cached summary predates the
revocation. The worker has access to both the corrected page and the stale
summary. The stale one is shorter and appears more relevant, so it wins the
retrieval score.

Nothing in this failure requires the model to be malicious. The system mixed
five different facts: material was stored, material was available to the
current task, material had once been used, material was believed, and material
was authorized. It treated them as one condition called memory.

A governed system needs a sharper boundary. **Virtual context** is the exact,
temporary view mounted for one consumer and purpose. **Durable semantic
memory** is the versioned set of objects and relations the system may carry
across tasks and restarts. Neither is truth. Neither is authority. Both need
identity, provenance, freshness, rights, contradiction, taint, revocation,
expiry, and residuals.

The release-note worker should receive a new context transaction. That
transaction asks for the current public trial result, its permitted evidence,
the active release policy, and known contradictions. The resolver sees that
the cached summary depends on a revoked raw path and an obsolete claim. It can
exclude the summary, mount it as quarantined diagnostic material, or request a
fresh derivation. If the summary had already become durable belief, the memory
layer must invalidate that belief and every known consumer receipt derived
from it.

This is more work than vector search. It is also narrower than a promise of
perfect memory. The architecture does not guarantee that all useful context is
found or that stored beliefs are true. It makes presence, use, belief, and
permission separate enough to challenge.

## Five States, Not One Memory

The word *memory* often collapses several systems that fail differently.

**Source state** contains the original files, observations, policies, messages,
datasets, traces, and records. A source may be authentic or forged, current or
stale, authorized or denied. Its existence does not determine its meaning.

**Storage state** records what bytes or structured objects are retained and
where. Databases, object stores, indexes, caches, model weights, backups, and
logs all belong here. Successful storage proves neither retrieval nor lawful
use.

**Context state** is what a particular consumer can see during a bounded
operation. It includes selected source spans, summaries, tool results,
policies, schemas, examples, and prior work. The context window is one physical
carrier for this state, not its complete semantics.

**Belief state** records which propositions, objects, relations, procedures,
or hypotheses the system is prepared to carry forward. Belief can be
qualified, contradicted, superseded, scoped, or unknown. Repetition and
retrieval do not create justified belief.

**Authority state** determines which material may influence which action for
which purpose. A belief can be well supported yet unauthorized for a consumer.
A private fact may be valid and still excluded from a public release. A tool
may be able to read a file without having permission to publish it.

The five states interact but do not inherit from one another. Storage does not
grant context admission. Context admission does not establish belief. Belief
does not grant authority. Authority does not establish truth. A useful memory
architecture keeps those failed implications visible in its records and APIs.

This separation also clarifies deletion. Removing an object from the active
context is not deleting storage. Deleting one database row is not removing a
backup. Removing exact bytes is not necessarily removing a learned influence
from model parameters. Revoking authority is not pretending the information
never existed. Each operation needs its own target and receipt.

## Context Is a Typed Mount

A context request should say more than “find relevant documents.” It identifies
the consumer, task, purpose, requested object or query family, source and time
boundaries, authority ceiling, freshness requirements, adequacy criteria,
conflict policy, loss tolerance, cost budget, lease, and failure behavior.

The resolver answers with a **mount**, a versioned view over admitted context
objects. The mount can contain exact source spans, typed records, derived
summaries, indexes, tool outputs, or references to material too large or
restricted to copy. Every item retains its source identity, transformation,
version, validity interval, rights, taint, and omission record.

For the release note, the request names the public-release consumer and current
trial-summary purpose. It requires the active release policy, public evidence,
the current controller identity, the observed stop condition, and open
residuals. It excludes raw private paths and claims beyond the bounded trial.
The context lease lasts for one draft-and-review transaction. It expires if the
policy, source page, evidence epoch, or consumer changes.

The mount is not a bag of text. It is a governed view. Two consumers can mount
different views over the same source estate. An internal investigator may see
the raw trace path; a public writer may see only an approved evidence link. A
verifier may need exact schema fields; a human reader may need a concise
explanation plus a rescue link. Those views can be equally legitimate without
being identical.

A mount can also be incomplete. The resolver records requested but absent
objects, unresolved aliases, omitted material, denied sources, stale items,
conflicts, failed retrievals, truncated fields, and approximations. Silence is
not evidence that the missing item does not exist.

## Pages, Cells, and Certificates

The Virtual Context ABI provides a shared record shape without requiring every
memory backend to use one physical layout.

A **page** groups context for a declared purpose and consumer. It has a stable
page identity, version, lease, source basis, authority ceiling, adequacy target,
and residual set. Pages can be mounted, superseded, invalidated, or released.

A **cell** is an addressable semantic item within or referenced by a page. It
may hold an exact value, proposition, relation, source span, procedure,
constraint, policy, observation, summary, or pointer. A cell records type,
identity, origin, transformation, time, uncertainty, rights, taint, and known
dependents. Its semantic identity remains distinct from its token position,
embedding, storage address, or cache key.

A **certificate** binds a materialized page to the request it answers. It lists
the resolver and version, source fingerprints, admitted and omitted cells,
losses, freshness, conflict disposition, authority checks, adequacy checks,
faults, costs, and lease. It may say that a page is structurally admissible for
one consumer. It does not certify that every cell is true or that the model
will use the page correctly.

This distinction lets different substrates share context. A graph store can
resolve relations, a vector index can propose related passages, a database can
return exact records, and a long-context model can consume rendered text. They
exchange pages, cells, and certificates while retaining their own storage and
retrieval methods.

The ABI should remain smaller than a universal ontology. It defines the fields
needed to preserve identity, boundaries, and repair. Domain schemas define
what a controller result, legal rule, biological observation, or financial
position means. If the ABI tries to encode every domain, it becomes the brittle
private language it was meant to avoid.

## Addresses Are Not Meaning

Every context system needs addressing, but no address is sufficient by itself.

A file path can change when a repository moves. A line number changes when a
paragraph is inserted. A content hash changes when formatting changes. A vector
address depends on an embedding model and index version. A database key can
survive while the row's meaning changes. A natural-language name can refer to
several objects.

The architecture keeps physical, content, structural, semantic, and authority
identities separate. A semantic object can map to several exact source spans.
One source span can support several propositions. A content hash binds bytes;
an alias record proposes co-reference; an authority record governs use. None
silently substitutes for the others.

The stale summary in the example has a valid content identity. It is not
corrupted bytes. Its problem is semantic and temporal: it refers to an obsolete
claim and carries denied provenance into a public consumer. Deleting it merely
because it is stale would also destroy useful diagnostic history. The better
response is to preserve its identity, mark its current disposition, block
ordinary use, and retain a governed repair path.

Stable identities make descendant invalidation possible. When the privacy
policy changes, the system can ask which cells, summaries, pages, prompts,
claims, artifacts, and consumer receipts depended on the newly denied source.
An approximate embedding search may help discover unrecorded descendants, but
declared lineage supplies the exact known set and exposes the remaining
discovery gap.

## Snapshots Freeze a View, Not the World

A snapshot records one context or memory state at a precise boundary. It binds
versions of sources, policies, indexes, aliases, rights, transformations,
resolvers, and unresolved residuals. It enables replay and comparison.

Snapshots are essential when work spans time. The release-note draft should be
reviewed against the same policy and evidence view used to create it, or the
system should explicitly rebase it onto a newer view. Without a snapshot, a
reviewer may approve text whose citations or permissions changed between draft
and review.

A snapshot does not freeze external reality. The underlying controller can
change, a source can be corrected, and a right can be revoked. The snapshot
remains a historical record of what the transaction saw. Its lease and
freshness rules determine whether it can still support action.

This creates two valid operations. **Replay** reconstructs a historical view
for diagnosis. **Refresh** resolves a new view under current state. Replaying an
old snapshot does not reauthorize its contents. Refreshing does not erase the
old basis. A governed system needs both to explain why a decision occurred and
why the same decision should or should not occur now.

## Context Changes Are Transactions

Mounting context changes the effective input to cognition. It should have
transaction semantics where consequences justify them.

A context transaction binds a request, base snapshot, proposed additions and
removals, source versions, policy epoch, resolver, conflict decisions,
authority checks, expected descendants, and commit conditions. It can prepare
a candidate page, validate it, commit a new mounted version, or abort without
presenting a half-updated view as current.

The transaction protects against a common hybrid state. Suppose the corrected
claim is mounted, but the old privacy policy remains cached. Or the policy is
current, but the embedding index still returns the denied path. A consumer can
receive pieces from incompatible epochs even though every component is valid
in isolation.

Atomicity is consumer-relative. A simple single-process store may use an
append-only event plus one pointer swap. A distributed context service may need
version vectors, leases, idempotent retries, conflict records, and compensating
actions. The architecture should not claim serializability or linearizability
without implementing and testing them. It must state what consistency model it
actually provides.

Crash behavior belongs in the contract. A crash before event append should
leave the old view current. A crash after append but before index update should
be recoverable through replay. A crash after materialization but before
consumer acknowledgment should not create an untracked use. Every ambiguous
boundary becomes a residual rather than an assumed success.

## Branches Need Context Isolation

Planning, search, simulation, and parallel work create branches with different
assumptions. One branch may use the corrected public evidence. Another may
inspect the stale summary to diagnose the earlier failure. A third may test a
hypothesis in which the controller really did identify oscillation safely. All
three branches can be useful. They cannot share one undifferentiated context.

Each branch receives its own snapshot identity, assumptions, mounted objects,
authority ceiling, writes, observations, and residuals. A hypothetical object
is typed as hypothetical even when its wording resembles an observed fact. A
diagnostic branch may read quarantined material without granting that material
ordinary publication use. A private branch can derive an internal finding
without making it available to the public branch.

Isolation is not automatically supplied by separate model calls. Two calls may
share a cache, retrieval index, scratch directory, tool session, or durable
memory writer. The transaction boundary must include every state carrier that
can move information between branches. Undeclared carriers become explicit
isolation residuals.

Joining branches is a semantic operation. The join compares base snapshots,
object identities, assumptions, policy epochs, rights, contradictions,
external effects, and writes. Exact nonconflicting records may merge
mechanically. Conflicting claims remain plural or route to adjudication.
Hypothetical facts do not become actual because several simulated branches
contain them. A denied source cannot enter the public branch through a summary
written by an internal branch.

The release-note task illustrates the rule. The diagnostic branch can preserve
the stale summary and its raw path to explain the defect. Its output is a
repair record whose public projection says only that restricted provenance was
removed. The public branch consumes that approved projection, not the
diagnostic context itself. Both branches retain lineage to the same incident
without inheriting the same view or authority.

Branch retirement matters too. When a search branch loses, its context should
not remain mounted indefinitely or silently consolidate into durable belief.
Useful negative evidence, failed hypotheses, and repair lessons can be proposed
for memory through a separate admission transaction. Temporary prompts,
credentials, private artifacts, and speculative assertions expire with the
branch unless another policy explicitly preserves them.

Strong isolation has costs. Copying every object is wasteful, while sharing
immutable content with copy-on-write views can be efficient. The implementation
may choose snapshots, overlays, namespaced caches, capability-scoped handles,
or transactional stores. The architectural requirement is observable: branch
identity and permitted information flow survive the optimization, and merge or
leakage failures can be detected.

## Taint Is a Dependency Property

Taint records a reason that material requires restricted handling. It may arise
from privacy, licensing, security classification, uncertain provenance,
untrusted generation, stale policy, contamination, adversarial input, failed
validation, or a known contradiction.

Taint is not a permanent moral label on bytes. It is typed, scoped, and
versioned. A private path and an unverified claim fail for different reasons.
One may be safely transformed into an approved public reference; the other may
require evidence or weaker wording. A declassification decision needs an
authorized rule and receipt. Merely paraphrasing tainted material does not
remove its lineage.

Propagation follows dependency, not textual similarity alone. If a summary
uses a denied source, the derived cell carries that dependency even when it
contains none of the source's exact words. If an aggregate can be released
under a validated privacy rule, the new artifact records the transformation,
allowed consumer, residual risk, and source obligations.

Overtainting can make a system unusable. Undertainting can leak restricted
material or launder unsupported claims. The remedy is not one global Boolean.
It is typed propagation, explicit declassification, consumer-specific rules,
and measurements of false blocks, missed dependencies, review burden, and
downstream harm.

## Durable Memory Begins With Events

Temporary context ends when the lease closes. Some results deserve to survive:
the corrected public claim, the active privacy policy, the relation between the
trial and its evidence, and the fact that a stale summary was rejected. Durable
memory admits these as versioned semantic objects and events.

An event-sourced design records admission, normalization, relation creation,
contradiction, supersession, rights change, retrieval use, correction,
compaction, migration, deletion request, and retirement. The current view is a
projection over that history, not an overwrite that destroys it.

Events help with replay and accountability, but logs are not automatically
truthful or complete. A missing event, forged actor, wrong timestamp, or bad
normalization can reproduce the same error deterministically. Event identity,
authorization, source binding, and validation remain separate requirements.

Durable objects retain semantic identity across representations. The
proposition that the bounded trial stopped after oscillation may appear in a
source note, claim ledger, public page, release note, and memory graph. Those
artifacts have different identities and consumers. Their shared proposition
identity allows correction to propagate without claiming that all wording is
equivalent.

## Knowledge Is a Lattice of Qualified Relations

Calling memory a *knowledge lattice* emphasizes that beliefs can be ordered,
related, revised, and viewed under different scopes without collapsing into
one canonical sentence.

Objects can represent entities, events, observations, claims, policies,
procedures, hypotheses, and artifacts. Relations name roles: source supports
claim, policy governs use, observation concerns controller, summary derives
from trace, claim supersedes claim, consumer used object. Provenance records
how each relation entered and which transformations it survived.

The lattice need not imply that every belief has a neat mathematical join.
Some conflicts should remain unresolved. One source may report that the
controller stopped because of oscillation while another attributes the stop to
a timeout. The system can preserve both observations, their scopes, and the
open adjudication rather than averaging them into a false consensus.

Consolidation creates a new derived object only when a policy states what may
be combined, which distinctions are preserved, what is lost, and which
consumers can use the result. The derived object keeps every parent source and
cannot inherit broader purpose authority than its parents permit.

This is controlled fallibility, not omniscience. The lattice should make it
possible to ask what was believed, why, under which ontology, for which
consumer, at which time, with which contradictions and omissions.

## Contradiction Is Not a Cache Miss

Retrieval systems often return the most similar or highest-ranked item. A
memory system also needs to return material conflicts.

Contradictions can be logical, temporal, observational, policy-based, or
identity-based. “The controller stopped” and “the controller continued” may be
inconsistent if they concern the same run and time. They may both be correct if
they concern different runs. A privacy policy can supersede an earlier policy
without making the historical policy false. Two aliases may refer to distinct
controllers despite similar names.

The contradiction record binds the compared objects, asserted relation,
scope, time, ontology, detection method, evidence, adjudication state, and
affected consumers. It can block strict use, permit a plural view, request
observation, or narrow the question.

Supersession also needs care. A newer object does not automatically dominate an
older one. Authority, evidence, scope, and effective time determine the
relation. The old object remains available for historical replay while current
consumers receive the new one.

In the release-note case, the corrected claim supersedes the stale summary for
public current use. The stale summary remains diagnostically relevant because
it explains the retrieval failure. The context certificate shows which one was
mounted and why.

## Retrieval Produces Candidates

Exact lookup, lexical search, vector retrieval, graph traversal, learned
navigation, long-context scanning, and hybrid methods are candidate generators.
They should be evaluated against the consumer's actual need.

A candidate passes through identity resolution, provenance, freshness,
contradiction, rights, taint, scope, relevance, and adequacy checks. The result
may be admitted, denied, quarantined, narrowed, or returned with unresolved
alternatives. A high similarity score cannot override a denied purpose or open
deletion duty.

The strongest baseline is not an intentionally naive vector store. It includes
competent databases, retrieval-augmented generation, graph retrieval, long
context, ordinary caches, rerankers, source citations, access control, and
human review. The governed layer must earn its extra state by improving useful
outcomes, correction, provenance survival, contradiction handling, rights
closure, or recovery after complete costs are counted.

Retrieval quality may dominate many tasks. If better indexing and reranking
solve the observed failures, the semantic layer should contract. Governance is
not an excuse to preserve a costly ontology that adds no decision value.

## Forgetting Has Several Targets

A request to forget can concern active context, a cache entry, durable storage,
an index, a backup, a derived summary, a consumer belief, a model parameter, an
external recipient, or future authority. Those targets are not interchangeable.

The system begins with a known-copy and known-descendant inventory. It records
what was requested, under which right or policy, which identities are in
scope, which operations ran, what was verified, what could not be reached, and
which residuals remain.

Removing the stale summary from the active context prevents immediate reuse.
Retiring its durable object prevents ordinary retrieval. Deleting its storage
copies changes retention. Invalidating descendant receipts tells known
consumers not to rely on it. None proves that every copy was found or that a
model's learned influence disappeared.

Machine unlearning belongs beside, but not inside, this lifecycle. A parameter
update can be evaluated for behavioral removal, influence, membership privacy,
lineage, storage, backups, descendants, and utility. Improvement on one axis
does not close the others. The memory ledger should preserve those separate
outcomes rather than issuing one “forgotten” flag.

Forgetting also has an epistemic cost. Deleting source material can make later
claims harder to audit. Rights and retention policy may require deletion
despite that cost. The architecture records the trade rather than silently
retaining information because it might be useful.

## Migration Must Preserve the Repair Path

Memory systems change. Ontologies evolve, indexes are rebuilt, embeddings are
replaced, storage backends migrate, schemas split, and models reinterpret old
records.

A migration packet maps old and new identities, fields, relations, ontology
versions, losses, conflicts, rights, consumers, and rollback conditions. It
tests exact records where possible and samples semantic behavior where exact
equivalence is unavailable. Every unresolved mapping becomes a residual.

Rollback is bounded by what changed externally. Reverting an index may restore
retrieval ordering. It cannot retract a release note already copied elsewhere.
Restoring a database snapshot may reintroduce a record that policy now denies.
A rollback therefore replays current authority and deletion rules rather than
pretending to return the world to an earlier state.

Migration quality is consumer-relative. A new embedding can preserve ordinary
question answering while losing rare contradiction retrieval. A compacted log
can preserve current values while losing why they changed. The acceptance test
must include the queries and repair duties important to known consumers.

## Failure Cases

**Presence laundering.** A stored or retrieved item is treated as true.

**Authority laundering.** A readable item is treated as permitted for the
current purpose.

**Epoch mixing.** A context combines sources, policy, aliases, or indexes from
incompatible versions.

**Stale summary dominance.** A concise derived object outranks a current exact
source.

**Positional identity.** Insertions or migrations detach repairs from their
semantic targets.

**Silent omission.** Missing, denied, truncated, or failed retrieval is
presented as an adequate complete view.

**Contradiction collapse.** Conflicting observations are averaged or one is
discarded without adjudication.

**Taint laundering.** Paraphrase or re-embedding hides restricted provenance.

**Taint explosion.** Broad propagation blocks unrelated uses and makes the
system unusable.

**Split transaction.** A consumer sees a new claim with an old policy or a new
policy with an old index.

**Replay reauthorization.** A historical snapshot is mounted as though its
expired rights were current.

**Alias collision.** Similar names or embeddings merge distinct entities and
their authority.

**Ontology migration loss.** A relation survives syntactically while its role
or scope changes.

**Deletion by count.** Matching an expected number of deleted objects is
treated as proof that the correct identities were removed.

**Behavioral-forgetting substitution.** A changed model answer is treated as
proof of parameter, storage, backup, legal, and descendant erasure.

**Unbounded context administration.** Provenance and certificates cost more
than the decision warrants.

## The Strongest Simpler Baseline

The strongest ordinary design uses versioned source control, a transactional
database, an object store, access control, exact and vector indexes, cache
invalidation, citations, retention jobs, and human review. It can solve many
problems without pages, cells, knowledge lattices, or a universal memory
service.

That baseline should be the default competitor. The governed architecture is
justified where several consumers need shared identity and repair across
temporary context and durable belief; where contradiction, rights, taint,
expiry, migration, or deletion materially affect decisions; or where replay
and descendant invalidation matter.

For low-consequence tasks, an ephemeral prompt assembled from current files
may be safer and cheaper. For exact records, a relational database may be more
reliable than semantic retrieval. For one user and one process, ordinary
transactions may supply enough consistency. The stack should not demand its
full memory protocol everywhere.

The comparison must count retrieval quality, downstream utility, correction
speed, false admission, false denial, provenance survival, contradiction
calibration, rights closure, deletion residuals, latency, storage, compute,
energy, implementation complexity, and human burden.

## What the Current Work Establishes

The three technical owners supply substantial finite record contracts, not a
deployed memory system.

The Virtual Context ABI has six implemented public proof targets and 83 live
Lean declarations. Its bounded surfaces include three valid and five rejecting
admission fixtures, two valid and nine rejecting resolver routes, one
four-project certificate with eleven rejecting mutations, a 39-theorem request
and fault lifecycle with 73 rejected mutations, and a reachable certificate
admission surface with 64 rejected mutations. Mixed QCSA results remain bounded
to their synthetic workloads.

Context Transactions has four implemented targets and 52 Lean declarations:
seventeen retained finite route and countermodel results plus 35 reachable
refinement declarations. Its executable records include three valid and six
rejecting store cases, two valid and four rejecting sequence cases, and one
bounded five-project restart lifecycle with ten rejecting mutations.

Durable Semantic Memory has one implemented target through a 35-declaration,
seven-transition review. Thirty-eight admission-axis mutations receive exact
repair or refusal dispositions. The model preserves identity, provenance,
purpose narrowing, migration invalidation, retrieval-use receipts, replay
composition, and open deletion-duty blocking inside authored finite records.
Two collision pairs separate contradiction state from a thin summary and
storage deletion from learned influence.

None of these results transfers support among the owners. All three cores
remain `Design rationale` at `argument`. They do not establish source truth,
context adequacy, useful retrieval, transaction isolation, serializability,
linearizability, crash durability, complete taint or deletion propagation,
behavioral forgetting, natural model use, safety, deployment, reproduction, or
transfer.

## From a Minimum Context Service to Durable Memory

A minimum implementation can use the release-note case. Create exact source,
policy, corrected-claim, stale-summary, and consumer identities. Issue a
public-purpose context request, resolve at least exact and semantic candidates,
materialize a page, record omissions and taint, and bind a certificate. Inject
a policy revocation and stale-index fault. Require the transaction either to
mount a coherent current view or fail with a typed residual.

Then admit only validated, authorized conclusions into a small event-sourced
semantic store. Record contradiction, supersession, retrieval use, correction,
and deletion duty. Crash before and after event append, projection update,
snapshot, compaction, and consumer receipt. Replay the event stream and compare
the exact governed view. Test known descendant invalidation without claiming
that the inventory is complete.

The next stage needs natural update-heavy tasks with changing sources,
conflicting observations, policy revisions, ontology migration, restarts,
compaction, poisoning, rights changes, deletion, and model replacement. Compare
exact databases, vector and graph retrieval, long context, ordinary RAG, and
human review under matched access and tuning. Score task utility and every
governance cost separately.

The mature service would provide temporary context and durable semantic state
to heterogeneous models, tools, agents, and institutions. It would support
plural ontologies and hypotheses, consumer-bound views, independently
replaceable retrieval backends, bounded consolidation, precise revocation,
rights-aware forgetting, restart recovery, and migration without pretending
that one graph or embedding is the world.

Maturity is not perfect recall. It is controlled fallibility: the system can
say what it mounted, what it believed, why, under which policy and ontology,
which contradictions survived, which consumers used it, what changed, and
what could not be repaired or forgotten.

## The Strongest Objection

Structured context and semantic memory can amplify an early mistake. A wrong
identity, relation, policy interpretation, or ontology mapping may propagate
farther because the system records it precisely. Rich certificates can create
false confidence while retrieval quality still determines whether the useful
fact reaches the model.

The objection has force. Governance metadata is not meaning. A perfect lineage
graph around a false proposition remains false. An expensive memory service
that retrieves worse context than a simple index can reduce system quality.
False precision also consumes reviewer attention and makes migrations harder.

The architecture responds by keeping ambiguity and contradiction first-class,
making retrieval backends replaceable, allowing thin implementations, and
requiring consumer-specific advantage. Stable identities make a mistake
repairable; they do not make it correct. Certificates report their checked
boundary; they do not certify truth.

Where simple retrieval, ordinary databases, access control, and cache
invalidation perform as well, the layer should contract. The most elaborate
memory machinery belongs only where shared identity, temporal revision,
rights, contradiction, replay, or descendant repair changes consequential
decisions.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

Simpler retrieval and memory systems matching provenance preservation,
contradiction handling, forgetting, transfer, revocation, recovery, and total
cost would justify a thinner layer. Evidence that stable semantic identity or
event history systematically worsens correction could retire those mechanisms
for affected workloads.

Evidence supporting the broader design would require prospective natural
campaigns against competent database, vector, graph, long-context, RAG, and
human-review baselines. They would need update-heavy tasks, complete event and
consumer denominators, independent outcome measures, crash and migration
faults, rights and deletion tests, causal ablations, reproduction, and transfer
across models, backends, domains, and organizations.

The conclusion should remain narrow if the layer improves auditability but not
useful outcomes, or if its governance burden exceeds the harms it prevents.
One clean replay cannot establish semantic continuity, and one retrieval win
cannot establish durable memory.

## What This Establishes

Context is a temporary, typed, consumer-bound mount. Durable memory is a
versioned history of qualified semantic objects and relations. Storage,
context, belief, and authority remain distinct.

Pages, cells, certificates, snapshots, transactions, taint, contradiction,
supersession, retrieval receipts, migration packets, and deletion residuals
give failures exact locations. They allow a stale summary to remain available
for diagnosis while preventing it from silently governing a public release.

The current finite proofs and fixtures show that these boundaries can be made
machine-checkable for authored records. They do not show that the resulting
system retrieves well, remembers truth, forgets completely, or works in
deployment.

When identity, authority, freshness, or contradiction cannot be resolved, the
safe result is not an empty context disguised as confidence. The transaction
returns the unresolved objects, denied operations, missing evidence, affected
consumers, and next admissible checks, then holds consequential use. A later
resolver can continue from that exact boundary without converting uncertainty
into absence.

Available information is not necessarily reviewable information. The next
unit asks how finite reviewer attention, evidence, objections, formal proofs,
runtime observations, and changing consumers can remain connected without any
one artifact standing in for the rest.
